Success means establishing a verifiable, audit-ready physical safety layer that aligns with EU AI Act frameworks and secures urban autonomy.
keywords: Urban Infrastructure, Neuromorphic Safety, Spatial Standards, Digital Twin Governance, Physical AI Compliance
rationale: Day-to-day urban operations and standard consultants lack the formal verification framework required for high-risk physical AI. An ETH domain researcher is crucial to bridge the gap between theoretical neuromorphic computing and rigorous urban safety proofs. We need specialized expertise in formal verification, real-time control safety, and spatial data modeling to mathematically validate our 6D geometric safety kernel. Rigorous academic research will transform our engineering prototype into an audit-ready, EU AI Act-compliant infrastructure that commercial consultants cannot independently certify.
role: As the project lead and systems architect, I bring the overarching architecture (ÉTÈ) focusing on neuromorphic-geometric safety and international spatial standards (OGC). I will provide the core technical framework, open-source integration pipelines (such as verl reinforcement learning shims), and our European research institute (Fraunhofer) validation pathways. Furthermore, I offer direct access to cross-border industry networks, pilot use cases in low-altitude and smart urban IoT scenarios, and bridging resources with global standards bodies. We will act as the bridge translating academic rigor into scalable, real-world urban infrastructure deployments.

name: NGO "World Beach Sports Federation"
title: Resilient Alluvial Geothermal & Solar Hybrid Heating for Lightweight Sports Infrastructure in Kyiv
summary: We operate a beach sports center in Kyiv featuring a lightweight, steel-frame tensile-membrane facility. Heating this space during wartime winter blackouts requires burning over 60 tons of wood pellets, causing high operational costs, carbon emissions, and severe logistical risks. Our objective is to design and model a resilient, low-carbon hybrid heating system. Partnering with ETH Zurich, we will research the integration of a shallow alluvial geothermal heat pump (utilizing the Dnipro River's shallow water tables) with our existing on-site Solar PV microgrid. The pellet boiler will serve strictly as a peak-shaving backup. Success looks like reducing seasonal biomass consumption from 60 tons to under 10 tons, achieving near-zero carbon heating, and securing a reliable, off-grid climate. This ensures a stable, year-round environment for our free adaptive beach sports and pickleball physical rehabilitation program for wounded Ukrainian war veterans.
keywords: Geothermal Heat Pumps, Hybrid Renewable Energy Systems, Decentralized Microgrids, Thermal Efficiency of Tensile Membranes, Veteran Adaptive Sports Rehabilitation
rationale: While we have operational and sports infrastructure expertise, we face a major technical knowledge gap: modeling transient heat losses in large-scale double-walled tensile membranes under dynamic wind/ambient conditions, combined with shallow alluvial groundwater geothermal heat exchange on riverbanks. Rigorous academic research from ETH is crucial to simulate these thermodynamics, model the soil-water heat-extraction capacity, and optimize the microgrid control algorithms for hybrid solar-geothermal-pellet integration. Standard commercial consultants lack the advanced simulation tools and scientific rigor required to design this innovative, resilient off-grid energy model for a conflict zone.
role: As the practice partner, NGO World Beach Sports Federation offers a fully operational 1.5-hectare riverfront Living Lab (SET Centre) directly on the alluvial quartz sands of Trukhaniv Island. We offer unrestricted access to this field site, existing infrastructure (including an operating Solar PV plant and a 60-ton pellet boiler system), real-time energy use data, and dedicated administrative staff time. Furthermore, we will leverage over $175,000 in-kind matching funds (land use, facilities, coaching staff hours). Finally, we offer a direct social impact channel, running free physical and mental rehabilitation programs for wounded Ukrainian veterans. We bridge the gap between cutting-edge Swiss engineering and real-world, crisis-resilient urban infrastructure implementation on the ground.

name: Weorchestrate
title: Digital Lifecycle Stewardship Framework for Circular Packaging
summary: The project aims to develop and test a digital lifecycle stewardship framework that manages products and packaging before they become waste. The challenge is that packaging placed on the market can become difficult to track once it leaves the point of sale, resulting in fragmented accountability, limited visibility of return and reuse, and reliance on downstream waste-management and statistical reporting. The proposed framework would connect product and packaging units to standards-based digital identities and lifecycle records, enabling verified return, reuse, recovery and end-of-life routing. The research would explore how such an interoperable system could support circular economy outcomes, producer accountability and more reliable lifecycle data within an urban context. A controlled pilot could test the framework with selected products, retailers and return points. Success would be demonstrated through measurable improvements in verified returns, lifecycle traceability, reuse and recovery data, and the feasibility of scaling the approach.
keywords: Circular economy; Digital lifecycle stewardship; Packaging traceability; Verified return; EPR
rationale: An ETH Domain researcher is crucial to co-develop and scientifically assess the framework, particularly its lifecycle governance model, interoperability with existing standards, verification mechanisms, and potential application in an urban context. The practice partner brings the real-world problem, local context, operational knowledge and stakeholder needs, while the ETH research partner would contribute scientific methodology, interdisciplinary expertise and independent evaluation. The collaboration would help translate the framework from a conceptual model into a researchable and testable approach, while identifying appropriate research questions, measurable indicators and a feasible pathway for controlled pilot testing and future scalability.
role: The ideal ETH Domain researcher would bring expertise in circular economy, digital infrastructure, lifecycle systems, research methodology and evaluation, helping us scientifically test and assess the Digital Stewardship Infrastructure Framework in an urban context. They would contribute to defining the research questions, methodology, measurable indicators and evaluation approach, and to assessing how the framework can generate reliable lifecycle data and support future scalability. As the practice partner and framework developer, we can contribute the existing framework and its underlying concepts, local knowledge and context, access to relevant stakeholders and potential pilot environments, and our time and expertise for co-design, field testing and validation. We can also support stakeholder engagement and provide the practical perspective needed to ensure that the research addresses a real-world need

name: Simon Kuznets Kharkiv National University of Economics - potential academic research partner, Kharkiv, Ukraine
title: Adaptive Immersive Environment for Workforce Training and Reskilling to Support Ukraine’s Recovery
summary: Ukraine’s recovery will require rapid reskilling and upskilling of people whose previous qualifications no longer match emerging labour-market and reconstruction needs, including veterans, displaced people, returnees and workers re-entering employment. The project will develop and validate research-based models and methods for adaptive immersive training, combining personalised learning pathways with AR/VR simulations, digital twins of professional situations, interactive tasks and AI-supported guidance. The research will address how training content, pace, difficulty and support can adapt to users’ prior experience, competency gaps and learning progress, and how immersive scenarios can support safe and repeatable practice of professional tasks. Together with an ETH Domain research team and a regional practice partner in Kharkiv, we will co-design and test selected use cases. Success means validated models, methods, design principles and prototype scenarios that provide a strong foundation for future implementation and scaling across Ukraine.
keywords: Adaptive immersive learning, Reskilling and upskilling, Extended Reality (XR/AR/VR), Human capital recovery, Workforce development
rationale: The project requires research-based methods for designing adaptive immersive reskilling that connect user profiles, competency gaps, personalised learning pathways and performance in simulated professional tasks. We are looking for an ETH Domain researcher with strong expertise in XR/VR, human-computer interaction, immersive simulation and experimental evaluation to co-develop and validate these methods. Their research contribution would strengthen the development of evidence-based models, design principles and prototype scenarios for adaptive immersive training and provide a strong foundation for future implementation and scaling in support of Ukraine’s recovery.
role: Our main need is a researcher with strong expertise in XR/VR, immersive simulation and human-computer interaction, ideally complemented by experience in adaptive learning or reskilling. The ETH Domain partner would contribute advanced methods for designing and evaluating immersive professional training scenarios and help validate the proposed models and design principles. S. Kuznets Kharkiv National University of Economics would contribute expertise in adaptive immersive learning, personalisation, educational digital twins, gamification and AI-supported learning, as well as existing conceptual and methodological groundwork. Together with a regional practice partner in Kharkiv, we can provide access to local reskilling needs, stakeholders, potential users and field settings for co-design and evaluation. We can also contribute staff time, research infrastructure and in-kind support to the collaboration.

name: Global Alliance - Cities4Children/Save the Children
countries: Vietnam; South Africa; Peru; Indonesia; Egypt; Albania; Kosovo
title: Cities for Children and youth
summary:
Today, most of the world’s children are growing up in cities and towns. Yet for too many children in low- and middle-income countries, urban life means inadequate housing, unhealthy living environments, limited and low quality learning, and few safe places to play and meet friends. With rapid urbanisation, growing inequality, and weak governance, children face a large number of challenges in cities.  Here is an article explaining 24 reasons why cities and towns must do better for children to ensure that every child can grow up healthy, safe, happy, and hopeful. [removed]
Save the Children operates in almost 100 countries and we are keen to collaborate with researchers who are interested in addressing a range of topics relevant for children in urban contexts, with a strong focus on the most marginalized children. Given the breadth of topics and countries where we work, we are keen to discuss preliminary ideas with researchers and with our country offices to see what is possible.
keywords: inclusive urban development; children; youth; families; slum upgrading; cities for children
rationale: A focus of research on children in cities in Africa, Asia and Latin America is sorely lacking. We are hoping to work with researchers to co-develop a policy and practice relevant research agenda.
role: An interest and track record on topics relevant to children and urban development. We can offer links with Save the Children country offices, their networks, access to the neighbourhoods where they work, some matching staff time. We also have leading researchers on various topics who are part of the Global Urban Team, who would be involved in the design and entire process.

name: UrbanEcho
countries: Ghana; Egypt; Croatia; Morocco; Peru; South Africa; Romania; Serbia; Vietnam; Tunisia; Slovenia; Czech Republic; Latvia; Kyrgyzstan; Indonesia
title: Data-driven urban decision support tools for inclusive and sustainable cities
summary:
Urban decision-makers often struggle with fragmented and disconnected data sources, making it difficult to evaluate policies, coordinate stakeholders, and translate research into practical action. This challenge affects city governments, infrastructure agencies, service providers, and residents, particularly in rapidly growing cities where decisions must be made under uncertainty.

This project aims to integrate diverse city data into a shared operational environment for analysis, scenario testing, and decision support. Working alongside researchers and city stakeholders, the platform will transform research outputs into practical workflows and tools that can support everyday planning and policy processes. Potential applications include decision workflows for mobility planning, infrastructure investment, service accessibility, climate resilience, and urban development interventions.
keywords: Urban Digital Twins and systems, Evidence-Based Planning, Urban Analytics, City Governance, Policy Decision Support
rationale: Urban planning decisions often involve complex trade-offs that are not fully understood or documented. An ETH researcher is essential to map infrastructure planning and governance processes, identify key decision points, and determine the data, models, and evidence required to support them. This requires rigorous research that goes beyond conventional consulting by generating transferable knowledge and scientifically grounded methodologies. Together, the researcher and UrbanEcho will translate these insights into digital workflows, decision-support tools, and urban digital twin capabilities that enable the local practice partners to apply research findings in their day-to-day planning and investment decisions.
role: We envision contributing expertise in urban digital twins, data integration, and decision-support platform development. UrbanEcho will provide the technical environment needed to combine fragmented urban data, operationalize research outputs, and translate them into practical tools that can support day-to-day planning and investment decisions.  Our ideal researcher would bring expertise in urban governance, infrastructure planning, decision analysis, participatory methods, and urban systems modelling. Their role would be to identify key planning decisions, map decision-making processes, determine the data and analytical methods required, and develop evidence-based approaches for evaluating interventions.  UrbanEcho will contribute platform development, technical staff time, urban analytics expertise, stakeholder engagement support, and access to a growing network of city, academic, and industry partners. Together, we aim to co-develop digital workflows that enable practice partners to apply research findings in real-world planning processes and scale successful approaches across multiple cities.

name: Zendra Haris Prasetya
title: Empowering Communities for Urban Resilience: A Comparative Model of Environmental Management Governance and Climate Preparedness in Bandung (Indonesia) and Kobe (Japan)
summary: Rapid urbanization and climate-related pressures are exposing weaknesses in how cities manage household waste, particularly in Indonesia, where municipal systems often depend on uneven community participation and fragmented local governance. This project aims to develop an adaptive, community-based environmental governance model by comparing waste management and resilience practices in Bandung, Indonesia, and Kobe, Japan. The partnership with researchers at Kobe University provides a distinctive opportunity to connect Japan’s mature community-based environmental governance experience with Bandung’s dynamic grassroots practices, enabling meaningful cross-context learning rather than simple policy transfer. Using a mixed-methods approach, the study combines household surveys, stakeholder interviews, focus groups, and comparative policy analysis to examine behavioral readiness, institutional coordination, environmental justice, and community participation. Success would mean producing an empirically grounded comparative governance model, practical policy recommendations, and transferable principles for strengthening source-level waste reduction, community resilience, and social inclusion.
keywords: Environmental Governance, Urban Resilience, Waste Management, Community Participation, Climate Adaptation
rationale: ETH domain researcher is crucial to advancing the project from a bilateral comparative study into a broader and more transferable urban research platform. The involvement would strengthen the analytical design, deepen cross-context comparison, and help test whether insights from Bandung and Kobe can inform wider urban settings. We particularly value expertise that can sharpen the integration of environmental governance, urban resilience, and community-level evidence within a rigorous comparative framework. ETH participation would also expand the project’s collaborative scope, enabling stronger methodological exchange, wider international learning, and a more robust basis for future joint research and policy engagement.
role: We envision contributing the empirical, institutional, and implementation foundation of the collaboration. Our team brings expertise in environmental governance, community-based waste management, urban resilience, and mixed-methods research, supported by established academic and practitioner networks in Indonesia and Japan. We can provide access to field sites in Bandung, community and municipal stakeholders, local research staff, and primary data collection, while our collaboration with Kobe University enables direct comparative learning from the Japanese context. We seek an ETH researcher with expertise in urban governance, sustainability transitions, resilience, or related comparative and evaluation methods who can help strengthen cross-context analysis and model development. Together, the partnership would combine locally grounded evidence with rigorous comparative research to generate findings that are scientifically robust, practically applicable, and transferable to other urban contexts.

name: National Territorial Planning Agency, Albania
title: Digitalization and Artificial Intelligence for Climate-Resilient Spatial Planning in Albania
summary: To analyze the readiness of AKPT's existing geospatial datasets and explore how artificial intelligence (AI) and satellite imagery can be integrated into current systems to model urban heat stress. Identifying data gaps in Albania’s most vulnerable urban areas (Tirana, Durrës, etc.). Developing a pilot algorithm or model (using open-source geospatial platforms) demonstrating how implementing green corridors or urban forests can lower local temperatures in a pilot neighborhood.
keywords: urban development, sustainability, cohesion and planning
rationale: AKPT wants to integrate advanced AI algorithms with GIS to simulate urban heat stress, requiring specialized skills in geospatial machine learning, climate modeling, and digital urban design to develop novel, peer-reviewed microclimate predictive models for localized impact. The provided text highlights AKPT's need for specialized expertise in integrating advanced AI with GIS to simulate urban heat stress, a capability not met by their current operations or standard consultants. To address this, AKPT requires collaboration with an ETH researcher who can co-develop novel, peer-reviewed microclimate predictive models. This expertise should come from departments like D-BAUG or D-ARCH, focusing on geospatial machine learning, climate modeling, and digital urban design to create a customized, actionable tool for scalable local impact based on complex climate data.
role: AKPT, Albania's national planning agency, seeks an ideal ETH researcher with expertise in geospatial machine learning, microclimate modeling, and evaluating Nature-Based Solutions. AKPT offers comprehensive GIS databases, direct connections with municipalities, and urban field sites for pilot testing, along with significant staff time and administrative support to ensure the project is demand-driven and collaboratively developed.

name: Institute for Urban Politics
title: Digital Tools for Citizen Engagement
summary:
The Republic of Serbia faces significant challenges in ensuring meaningful public participation in planning processes. This is partly because the initial stages of participation, particularly informing and communicating with the public, are often insufficiently transparent and difficult for citizens to understand. In spatial and urban development, local civil society organisations (CSOs) and neighbourhood groups have become important actors in communicating planning information. However, many lack the capacity to continuously monitor planning processes and respond in a timely manner.

This project explores how digital technologies can support these actors in overcoming such capacity constraints and improve access to planning information. It aims to identify practical digital approaches that strengthen their ability to inform citizens and create better conditions for meaningful participation.

The research will (1) evaluate existing practices for informing the public about planning processes; (2) engage CSOs through a focus group to identify needs, barriers and opportunities; and (3) develop potential digital solutions for future implementation and testing.
keywords: Participatory Planning; Digital Technologies; Urban Development
rationale: After 15 years and work with over 100 community groups, we have tried many approaches to informing and engaging citizens in planning, adapting pragmatically to circumstances, but never systematically evaluated what actually drives understanding and sustained participation. That gap sits beyond daily practice or a short-term consultant: it needs rigorous, comparative research into digital participation tools, including why our outreach still skews toward users over 45 with limited digital literacy beyond social media. An ETH researcher brings the research design and evaluation expertise to turn 15 years of practice-based experience into an evidence base for future digital tool guidelines.
role: We need a researcher in digital civics: evaluation research at the intersection of social and political science and human-computer interaction, who can help us understand what works and what doesn't in informing and engaging citizens, and what should be tested in outreach and technology to be applicable for Serbia in 2027. We already have in-house capacity to build digital tools; what we lack is the evidence base to shape them meaningfully.  We bring 15 years of grassroots practice and multiple tested methodologies, direct access to neighborhood groups and interested citizens across Serbia as field sites for testing, communication channels for civic informing already recognised by the wider public, and a network of urban planners, activists and NGO professionals. Of our 7 staff, 4 work directly with people in the field and would be directly involved in this research, providing dedicated staff time throughout the project.

name: U-Nation
title: Investment and innovation readiness of Ukrainian urban recovery projects
summary: Key Research Question: How can Ukrainian cities increase the investment and innovation readiness of recovery projects and bridge the gap between local needs and the requirements of international investors, financial institutions, technology companies, and implementation partners? The logic of the research program: Research → Investment Readiness Assessment → identification of gaps → search for European innovations → finalization of projects → international validation → investment and innovation readiness. As a result, the program should create a practical mechanism that will help transform the needs of Ukrainian cities → into high-quality projects → integrate relevant European innovations into them → increase their investment readiness → create a basis for financing and further implementation.
keywords: Investment, innovation, international partnership, recovery
rationale: Gap: lack of research methodology. The research should be large-scale and focused on many aspects at the same time: identification of typical barriers that prevent urban projects from moving from an idea or concept to financing and implementation, investigation how the integration of modern technologies, solutions and practices of European cities and companies can increase the investment readiness of Ukrainian projects and their attractiveness for partners. Requirements from researcher: experience in strategic urban planning, in investment readiness, preparation of urban and infrastructure projects, networt among Swiss and international investors, ability to connect Ukrainian recovery projects with Swiss technologies and financing opportunities.
role: Ideal reseacher would bring academic leadership, international comparative analysis, data evaluation and scientific validation. From our side we can offer  a database of 40-60 real projects, their initial technical assessment of projects, working directly with cities, involving network of stakeholders, European cities, investors, companies and experts, staff time.

name: Odessa 5T
title: AI-Driven Waste Valorisation in Odesa
summary: The accumulation of construction waste and war-related debris in Odesa presents a critical opportunity to recover, recycle, and reuse materials to support reconstruction through waste valorisation. To make this process faster and safer, we propose developing a practical, AI-powered software solution designed to automate waste identification, segregation, and recovery at demolition and debris sites. Using image recognition and machine-learning, site managers can capture images of materials, such as bricks and metals, to pre-identify historical origin, screen for toxicity, and evaluate viability for upcycling into new construction materials. Starting with a pilot focused on a single material type, the project can be further scaled up to broader material classes. By streamlining waste collection and sorting, this technology aims to minimise manual labor, accelerate clearing of debris, and drive circular practices into Odesa’s urban restoration.
keywords: AI-Driven Waste Valorisation, Circular Reconstruction, Sustainable Urban Recovery, Digitalisation
rationale: The ETH domain researcher provides the necessary technical capacity and specialised know-how in waste valorisation and basic machine learning to build AI models that could accurately identify materials, screen for toxicity, and ensure the successful implementation of circular reconstruction in Odesa.
role: As an Odesa-based implementation partner, we bring direct access to local field sites and operational networks to host the project’s pilot and testbed environment. In return, we envision our role as the primary operational co-creator, ensuring the AI-driven software is continuously refined, tested, and validated in real-world conditions before scaling it across broader material classes and restoration sites. To complete this collaboration, our ideal ETH domain researcher brings specialised subject matter expertise in demolition waste valorisation, combined with machine learning, image recognition modeling, and toxicity screening methodologies. While they lead the technical architecture and model training, we can provide the practical testbed required to co-develop, deploy, and scale up this solution safely and effectively across Odesa.

name: Manado City
title: Nature-based Solutions for Riparian Restoration and Flood Mitigation in Manado
summary: The expansion of commercial and residential areas along the riparian zones of major rivers in Manado, including the Tikala, Tondano, and Sario, have caused recurring floods particularly during heavy and prolonged rainfall. This expansion has led to progressive river narrowing and severe sedimentation, significantly reducing buffer zones and the waterways' capacity to manage excess water. To strengthen the riparian restoration efforts and establish a more robust buffer zone, we propose a combined laboratory and pilot study to test fast-growing woody vegetation species capable of mitigating and slowing sedimentation rates. The findings from this study will then inform a policy brief submitted to local government authorities to enhance their river revitalisation strategy.
keywords: Nature-based solutions, Flood mitigation, Riparian restoration, River renaturation
rationale: Co-developing this project with an ETH Domain researcher, specifically from the Swiss Federal Institute for Forest, Snow and Landscape Research (WSL), is crucial due to their world-leading expertise in soil bioengineering, natural hazard mitigation, and plant ecology. Given Switzerland's extensive experience in managing severe flooding and erosion, a WSL researcher brings vital technical capabilities in evaluating fast-growing woody vegetation, plant-soil mechanics, and sediment dynamics. Their participation ensures rigorous laboratory and field methodology to test optimal species for riparian restoration.
role: As the local lead, I drive field operations, stakeholder coordination, and policy translation in Manado. I offer direct access to pilot sites along the three rivers, established government networks, land-use data, and dedicated staff time.  The ideal ETH Domain researcher brings complementary expertise in soil bioengineering, natural hazard modeling, and plant-soil mechanics, alongside rigorous methods for evaluating fast-growing woody vegetation to slow down sedimentation rates.

name: North-West University
title: Solar Cities and Regions: Policy innovation for accelerated urban and regional solar energy adoption in South Africa (North Cape)
summary: South Africa possesses some of the world's most exceptional solar resources, particularly in the Northern Cape. Nevertheless, municipalities continue to face challenges, including energy insecurity, ageing infrastructure, reliance on electricity sales for revenue, and limited policy capacity to promote distributed renewable energy generation. Cities and regions are increasingly recognised as vital stakeholders in the energy transition. Municipal governments can influence the adoption of solar energy through mechanisms such as zoning regulations, building codes, municipal procurement procedures, tariff structures, permitting processes, and local investment incentives. However, there remains insufficient evidence regarding which policy combinations are most effective, equitable, and scalable in the South African context.
keywords: spatial planning policy; green energy; underdeveloped region
rationale: Switzerland’s urban planning and solar energy framework appears to integrate energy mandates directly into spatial planning laws. Any new building with a rooftop or facade exceeding 300 square metres must install a solar energy system. This change affects spatial planning for large urban and regional projects. Switzerland also uses spatial planning laws to reduce bureaucratic hurdles for solar installations. The Federal Act on Spatial Planning states that certain solar systems do not require a standard, time-consuming building permit. Practical knowledge of how these policies are implemented would add tremendous value to the proposed study area.
role: The Northern Cape Province is South Africa's largest, but least developed region. However, it has the most potential for solar development initiatives given its location and physical characteristics. We have been conducting spatial planning projects in this province for 20 years and have built a significant institutional network. Numerous large-scale solar projects have been developed in this province, but they are focused on feeding energy into the national grid. There is no initiative to integrate green energy into spatial planning policy and legislation, and this proposed pilot project would investigate its feasibility.

name: Office for European Integration and Development
title: Smart, Energy-Efficient and Human-Centred Urban Lighting for Ivano-Frankivsk
summary: Ivano-Frankivsk needs to modernize its urban lighting system to improve energy efficiency, safety, accessibility and the quality of public spaces. The city is interested in moving from conventional lighting infrastructure towards a smart, adaptive and data-driven system that responds to pedestrian flows, mobility patterns, safety needs and energy constraints. The project would assess the existing lighting infrastructure, identify priority areas and develop a research-based model for modern urban lighting, including energy-efficient technologies, adaptive lighting, smart controls and data-driven planning. Particular attention would be paid to the relationship between lighting, pedestrian safety, accessibility, urban mobility and the attractiveness of public spaces. The expected result is a replicable model and evidence-based recommendations for phased investment in smart urban lighting, supporting both municipal decision-making and future EU-oriented urban development projects
keywords: Smart city; urban lighting; energy efficiency; public space; urban safety
rationale: The project requires research expertise that goes beyond the technical replacement of lighting equipment. We need to understand how lighting technologies, energy consumption, pedestrian behaviour, safety and public-space design interact. An ETH-domain researcher could contribute expertise in smart-city systems, urban modelling, energy efficiency, spatial analysis and evidence-based evaluation. Research could help identify optimal lighting scenarios, model energy and operational impacts, and assess how different lighting configurations affect safety, accessibility and urban activity. This would allow the city to move from infrastructure renewal towards a scientifically grounded and measurable urban lighting strategy
role: The Office can provide the researcher with access to the local urban context, municipal stakeholders, relevant city departments and potential infrastructure partners. We can facilitate access to available data on the existing lighting network, energy consumption, public spaces, mobility patterns and priority urban areas, subject to applicable data-access rules. The Office can also support field research, stakeholder interviews, pilot-site identification and engagement with the municipality and local community. We can help translate research findings into practical municipal recommendations and investment concepts, identify potential EU funding opportunities, and support communication with local decision-makers. Our contribution would therefore bridge scientific research and real-world urban implementation

name: Office for European Integration and Development
title: Designing an Inclusive City: Evidence-Based Accessibility and Inclusive Sports Spaces
summary: Ivano-Frankivsk is seeking to strengthen accessibility and inclusion as fundamental principles of urban development and reconstruction. The challenge is to move from individual accessibility interventions towards a systematic approach in which public spaces, pedestrian routes, recreational areas and sports infrastructure are designed around the needs of diverse users. The project would investigate barriers experienced by people with disabilities, older people, children and other groups with different mobility and sensory needs, and develop an evidence-based framework for inclusive urban design. Particular attention would be given to inclusive sports and recreation facilities that can be safely and meaningfully used by people with different physical abilities. Through spatial analysis, user research and participatory design, the project would identify priority interventions and develop principles, indicators and pilot solutions for inclusive public spaces. The expected outcome is a practical model that can guide future municipal planning, investment and urban reconstruction
keywords: Inclusive urbanism; accessibility; universal design; inclusive sports; public space
rationale: Creating genuinely inclusive urban environments requires more than applying accessibility standards. We need research to understand how spatial design, mobility patterns, user behaviour and different physical and sensory needs interact in real urban environments. An ETH-domain researcher could contribute expertise in universal design, urban planning, spatial analysis, mobility, human-centred research and participatory methods. Research could help develop measurable accessibility indicators, identify systemic barriers and evaluate alternative design solutions. This would enable the city to establish an evidence-based approach to inclusion rather than relying solely on individual infrastructure projects or compliance-based assessments
role: The Office can provide access to the local urban context and facilitate cooperation with municipal departments responsible for urban planning, infrastructure, social policy, sports and public spaces. We can support fieldwork, accessibility audits, user interviews and participatory workshops involving residents and relevant community organisations. The Office can help identify potential pilot locations, facilitate communication with decision-makers and coordinate local stakeholders. We can also support the translation of research findings into municipal planning tools, project concepts and investment proposals. Our European-integration role provides an additional platform for aligning the proposed model with European approaches to accessibility, inclusion and sustainable urban development

name: Office for European Integration and Development
title: Resilient Urban Healthcare: Integrating Health System Needs into City Reconstruction
summary: The reconstruction of Ukrainian cities creates an opportunity to rethink healthcare not only as a network of medical facilities but as an essential component of resilient urban development. Ivano-Frankivsk needs a research-based approach to planning healthcare infrastructure and services in relation to demographic change, population mobility, emergency risks, accessibility and the changing needs of residents. The project would analyse how healthcare facilities and services are distributed across the urban area, identify spatial and functional gaps, and develop scenarios for a more resilient and accessible urban healthcare system. Particular attention would be paid to the relationship between healthcare, transport accessibility, emergency preparedness, social infrastructure and population needs. The objective is to develop a model and set of planning indicators that can support municipal decisions on healthcare infrastructure, investment priorities and reconstruction. The approach could provide a transferable framework for other Ukrainian cities facing similar reconstruction and resilience challenges
keywords: Urban health; healthcare resilience; reconstruction; accessibility; spatial planning
rationale: The project requires interdisciplinary research linking urban planning, spatial analysis, healthcare systems, demographic modelling and resilience planning. The key knowledge gap is how to translate changing population needs and risks into optimal spatial and infrastructural configurations of urban healthcare. An ETH-domain researcher could contribute advanced methods for spatial modelling, accessibility analysis, scenario development and evidence-based planning. Research could identify underserved areas, model future demand and test alternative infrastructure and service scenarios. This would provide a stronger analytical basis for municipal investment decisions than conventional facility-by-facility planning
role: The Office can facilitate cooperation with the municipality, healthcare institutions, urban-planning authorities and other relevant stakeholders. We can support access to available spatial, demographic, infrastructure and service-delivery data and facilitate field research and stakeholder consultations. The Office can help identify priority urban areas and potential pilot cases, organise engagement with local decision-makers and translate research outputs into practical municipal strategies and investment concepts. We can also contribute expertise in European integration, project development and funding opportunities, helping connect the research findings with European reconstruction, resilience and urban-development priorities and potential financing instruments

name: Ternate City
title: Smart Early Warning System for Disaster Resilience in Ternate
summary: As an island city, Ternate is highly vulnerable to natural hazards, particularly tidal flooding, landslides, and earthquakes. Despite these recurring threats, its Early Warning System (EWS) remains underdeveloped. To advance disaster mitigation and support Ternate's vision as a resilient Smart Island, we propose developing an integrated spatial intelligence application that integrates multi-layered geographic data, including land-use patterns, land morphology, topographic conditions, and designated hazard zones, based on Ternate’s updated Regional Spatial Plan (RTRW). The platform will run predictive risk evaluations to generate real-time spatial visualisations, enabling municipal authorities to dynamically identify safe assembly areas and determine the most effective evacuation routes during emergencies. To ensure seamless adoption, the project incorporates targeted technical assistance and training for local government agencies, improving emergency communication protocols and public disaster risk literacy. Together, these interventions will optimise municipal response, strengthen early action, and safeguard lives and infrastructure across Ternate.
keywords: Early Warning System, Spatial Intelligence, Disaster Resilience
rationale: Co-developing this project with an ETH domain researcher, particularly from the Swiss Federal Institute for Forest, Snow and Landscape Research WSL, is essential to bridge critical expertise gaps in multi-hazard modeling and spatial planning. While routine operations manage basic responses, WSL offers advanced scientific capabilities to simulate complex natural hazards, model risk dynamics, and develop reliable predictive forecasting. Their expertise would be vital for converting multi-layered geographic data into a robust spatial intelligence application, while their recognition and experience in socio-institutional analysis ensures the platform seamlessly aligns with local government protocols, effective evacuation routing, and community disaster literacy.
role: As the project lead, we provide the operational foundation through primary spatial data, local governance networks, active field sites, and dedicated staff time. We will facilitate stakeholder coordination, field validation, and the delivery of technical assistance and community literacy programs. Meanwhile, the ideal ETH domain researcher brings advanced subject matter expertise in multi-hazard modeling, predictive risk evaluation, and spatial forecasting methods. They will supply the computational framework needed to process complex geographic and land-use layers into real-time visualisations.Together, this collaboration bridges local operational access with world-class scientific modeling to deliver an actionable spatial intelligence platform for disaster resilience.

name: Sukabumi City
title: Clean Water for Sukabumi: Modular Rainwater Harvesting and River Water Filtration
summary: The availability of clean water in Indonesia's Sukabumi Regency is increasingly becoming critical as upstream stone quarry waste renders the Cibojong River excessively turbid and unusable. This scarcity worsens during dry seasons, leaving local households without essential water for daily needs. To address this challenge, we propose conducting a pilot across selected riverside households to test portable roof-connected rainwater collection units integrated with modular Slow Sand Filtration (SSF) kits. Utilising locally accessible media including gravel, sand, activated carbon, and zeolite, these standalone filtration systems will treat harvested water and river water to improve local supply quality without requiring permanent construction. To ensure long-term operational sustainability, the pilot incorporates community capacity building and technical knowledge transfer. Community members will receive practical training on system assembly, filter media replacement, and routine operation and maintenance, empowering households to independently maintain the units.
keywords: Water Scarcity, Rainwater Harvesting, Community Capacity Building
rationale: An ETH Domain researcher, for example from Eawag, would be able to provide specific expertise in decentralised water treatment, low-cost filter design, and community-based maintenance models. Their scientific validation ensures the pilot delivers safe water year-round while equipping Sukabumi households with an easily maintainable, long-term solution.
role: As local implementers, we provide direct field access in Sukabumi, established community networks, dedicated staff time, and ground-level project management. We handle local stakeholder engagement, site coordination, and the execution of household pilot installations and training programs. To complement our field presence, our ideal ETH researcher brings specialised subject matter expertise in decentralized water treatment, filter performance modeling, and rigorous water quality evaluation. While the ETH researcher ensures technical reliability and filter optimisation for dual-source water, our team drives community adoption and long-term operational sustainability on the ground, delivering a scientifically proven, locally owned water solution.

name: Tazar Kyrgyzstan
title: Quantifying Consumption-Based Emissions Reduction Through Circular Resource Matching in Bishkek
summary: Bishkek faces growing waste volumes and limited formal recycling infrastructure. Over five years, Tazar has built grassroots circularity in the city through a mobile platform matching waste producers with recyclers, and through the Trash Festival, an annual environmental education event mobilizing residents around sustainable consumption. This activity generates rich transactional data material types, volumes, and matching outcomes, but has never been translated into a credible emissions metric. This pilot applies Life Cycle Assessment and Material Flow Analysis methods, in partnership with ETH Zurich's Chair of Ecological Systems Design, to quantify the consumption-based and indirect emissions avoided when material is diverted from landfill back into circulation rather than replaced by virgin extraction. The project will produce a first defensible emissions-avoidance estimate for Tazar's Bishkek operations, identify data gaps to strengthen future measurement, and build a replicable methodology for community-level circular economy initiatives across Kyrgyzstan and comparable urban contexts.
keywords: urban resource circularity, consumption based emissions, life cycle assessmment, circular economy
rationale: Tazar has five years of operational data from its waste-matching platform and Trash Festival programming, but no methodological tool to translate that activity into a credible emissions metric. This is precisely the knowledge gap: quantifying consumption-based and indirect emissions avoided through circular resource matching requires Life Cycle Assessment and Material Flow Analysis expertise that day-to-day operations or a general consultant cannot provide. We need a researcher skilled in LCA/MFA methods, supply-chain emissions modelling, and data-driven environmental impact quantification, specifically ESD's demonstrated expertise in applying these methods to consumption patterns and material flows.
role: Tazar brings five years of real-world operational data from an active circular-economy platform in Bishkek material types, volumes, and matching outcomes an asset few academic partners could otherwise access. We offer established community trust and mobilization capacity through the annual Trash Festival, giving the project a ready channel for translating research findings into public communication and behavior change. Our team contributes staff time for data preparation, cleaning, and contextual interpretation of Bishkek's waste and recycling landscape, along with in-kind support through our existing networks of waste producers, recyclers, and community partners (including women's cooperatives). As the non-academic practice partner, we ensure the research remains grounded in operational reality and generates outputs immediately usable for advocacy, future funding applications, and scale-up  rather than a purely academic exercise.

name: IzzyBike – Independent Inventor Project
title: Reinventing Urban Cycling: Experimental Evaluation of a Novel Chainless Front-Wheel-Drive Bicycle to Overcome Technical and Behavioural Barriers to Everyday Cycling
summary: Everyday urban commuters often face practical barriers to cycling, including limited storage space, theft risk, discomfort, and the inconvenience of using a conventional bicycle alongside public transport or work routines. These barriers can discourage people from choosing cycling for daily trips, limiting its contribution to sustainable urban mobility. The project is initiated by Marek Jurek, an independent inventor and engineer who created and patented IzzyBike, a chainless front-wheel-drive bicycle with rapid folding and an unconventional riding position. A research team at Poznan University of Technology is preparing comparative energy-demand testing and a dedicated test stand. The proposed collaboration would expand this work through laboratory and real-world testing of several prototype configurations, assessing energy efficiency, rider effort, ergonomics, stability, comfort, convenience and user acceptance. Success would mean robust evidence on whether this architecture can deliver measurable benefits and reduce barriers to everyday urban cycling.
keywords: Urban mobility, Active mobility, Bicycle engineering, Human factors and ergonomics, User acceptance
rationale: An ETH-domain researcher is crucial because the key gap is not product development, but rigorous scientific evidence on how IzzyBike performs and is experienced compared with conventional bicycles. Research can reveal relationships between bicycle configuration, rider effort, ergonomics, stability and user acceptance that prototyping or consultancy cannot establish reliably. We seek expertise in experimental design, human factors, mobility behaviour and quantitative analysis, complemented where relevant by biomechanics or bicycle dynamics. The researcher would co-design test protocols, define meaningful outcome measures, interpret results objectively and help translate the findings into evidence-based design improvements and credible conclusions for urban mobility.
role: We bring a mature technological concept, a functioning prototype and more than a decade of iterative engineering development. Marek Jurek, the inventor and engineer behind IzzyBike, will contribute his technical expertise, design know-how and detailed understanding of the bicycle’s unconventional drivetrain, geometry, folding mechanism and manufacturing challenges. We can provide access to the prototype, technical documentation, background IP and the possibility to modify or build experimental configurations in response to research findings. We also bring an established relationship with a research team at Poznan University of Technology, which is preparing comparative energy-demand testing and a dedicated test stand. Our contribution would therefore combine technology access, inventor expertise, engineering support and substantial in-kind involvement, enabling the ETH partner to test hypotheses on a real, technically mature mobility innovation rather than on a purely conceptual design.

name: Institution "Agency of Regional Development in Ternopil Region"
title: Support for small and medium-sized enterprises that have relocated or been affected by the war
summary:
The war has forced thousands of small and medium‑sized enterprises (SMEs) to relocate or operate under severe disruption. Many have lost access to local markets, supply chains, and infrastructure, while owners - often displaced families, women, and veterans’ households - struggle to preserve livelihoods. At stake is not only the survival of individual businesses but also the stability of regional economies and the jobs that sustain communities.

Our initiative seeks to provide targeted institutional support, financial tools, and capacity‑building programs that enable SMEs to adapt and recover. By strengthening relocated enterprises and helping war‑affected businesses rebuild, we aim to safeguard employment, foster innovation, and promote resilience. The ultimate goal is to transform vulnerability into opportunity - ensuring that SMEs remain engines of local development and contribute to long‑term economic cohesion despite the challenges of war.
keywords: SMEs,  Business relocation, Economic recovery, Regional development
rationale: A researcher from the ETH Domain is crucial because our work faces a knowledge gap in measuring the long‑term resilience of SMEs displaced or disrupted by war. Day‑to‑day operations and consultancy provide immediate solutions, but they cannot generate rigorous evidence on systemic impacts, adaptation models, or policy relevance. ETH expertise in applied economics, innovation systems, and quantitative methods will reveal patterns of recovery and relocation that practice partners alone cannot capture. We require advanced skills in data analysis, impact evaluation, and comparative research to co‑develop evidence‑based strategies for sustainable SME support in Ternopil region.
role: As the Agency of Regional Development in Ternopil Region, our value in this collaboration lies in providing direct access to local knowledge and networks. We hold up‑to‑date information on the economic situation in the region and maintain established contacts with all consolidated territorial communities. This allows us to connect research findings with the realities faced by SMEs that have relocated or been affected by the war. The ideal ETH researcher would bring expertise in applied economics, resilience modelling, and evaluation methods. Together, we can combine rigorous academic analysis with practical regional data and stakeholder engagement, ensuring that the project delivers evidence‑based solutions tailored to local needs.

name: Institute of National Planning
title: Enabling Local Energy Communities in Egypt through Regulatory Reform
summary: Despite its exceptional solar irradiance, Egypt’s distributed renewable energy market remains largely underutilised. The existing 1:1 net metering model supports initial growth, but threatens long-term grid stability and risks utility cost-recovery challenges as capacity expands. Transitioning toward a Net Billing mechanism backed by energy cooperatives offers a sustainable pathway to align decentralised generation with grid demand. However, Egyptian regulations lack a legal framework to recognise energy communities, preventing peer-to-peer power trading and collective billing aggregation. Drawing from Switzerland’s established Net Billing model and Local Electricity Communities (LEGs), this project aims to bridge Egypt’s regulatory gap. Working with local energy organisations, we propose to benchmark Swiss policy transferability, engage stakeholders, and draft a policy brief for the Egyptian Electricity Regulatory Authority (EgyptERA) to establish a legal foundation for energy cooperatives in Egypt.
keywords: Net Billing, Energy Cooperatives, EgyptERA Policy Reform, Energy Trading
rationale: An ETH domain researcher could provide critical technical and regulatory expertise on Switzerland’s Net Billing model and Local Electricity Communities (LEGs). Their background enables rigorous benchmarking of market mechanisms and grid integration standards. Additionally, ETH researchers could bring proven methodologies for policy transferability, energy economics, and stakeholder engagement. Working alongside Egyptian partners, the ETH researcher will be able to bridge theoretical Swiss policy with practical local implementation, ensuring the proposed policy brief for EgyptERA is rooted in empirical best practice and tailored to Egypt's specific grid context.
role: We envision a collaborative partnership where the ETH researcher provides leading subject-matter expertise in Swiss Net Billing mechanisms and Local Electricity Communities (LEGs), alongside methodological guidance in policy benchmarking, regulatory transferability, and energy economics modeling. In turn, our local organisation offers deep contextual knowledge of Egypt’s power sector, dedicated staff time, access to national solar market data, and established networks with key stakeholders. We will also host co-design policy workshops and coordinate local stakeholder engagement. By combining ETH's technical rigor in decentralised energy frameworks with our local institutional access and field capabilities, we believe we can deliver a robust, contextualised policy brief to establish a legal foundation for Egyptian energy cooperatives.

name: National Network of Local Philanthropy Development
title: Models of Financial Independence for Ukrainian Community Foundations
summary:
Our organization is a network of community foundations (CFs) across Ukraine, uniting 22 CFs. In the context of prolonged war, when most local resources are directed toward supporting the army, CFs largely depend on grant funding from international donors. This creates a structural dependency on donor priorities and shifting international agendas, making long-term planning difficult.

We are seeking to develop a sustainable, independent financing model for community foundations — one that reduces reliance on external grants and builds resilient local income streams. Promising directions include social enterprise models and decentralized renewable energy infrastructure, such as solar power stations built through community or cooperative ownership (e.g., on garage cooperatives or apartment building rooftops), with energy sold to local residents or businesses.

We are looking for a researcher from the ETH domain interested in studying financial sustainability models for CFs in Ukraine.
keywords: Сommunity foundations, financial sustainability, social enterprise, decentralized energy, Ukraine recovery
rationale: Our knowledge gap is methodological: we lack rigorous evidence on which financing structures allow community foundations to remain mission-driven nonprofits while building sustainable working capital, rather than converting into commercial enterprises. Day-to-day operations and consultants can propose ad hoc solutions, but cannot systematically test community willingness to co-invest, compare financing models (grants, blended finance, impact investment) across contexts, or design governance safeguards preserving nonprofit status. Community foundations are already driving Ukraine's wartime recovery — their resilience now depends on capital, not goodwill alone. We require an ETH researcher skilled in development finance, governance design, and empirical field methods to identify and validate models transferable to the Ukrainian context.
role: Our ideal researcher would bring expertise in development finance, governance design, and empirical field methods — particularly experience evaluating financing models (blended finance, impact investment, cooperative structures) in fragile or conflict-affected contexts, along with skills in field survey design and financial modeling.  As a network of community foundations across Ukraine, we bring practical value that a researcher could not access independently. Beyond our team's time and expertise, we can organize direct engagement on the ground: facilitating fieldwork and household surveys within communities, connecting the researcher with residents willing to discuss investment readiness, and coordinating with local self-government and state authorities where relevant. Our established trust within communities — built through years of grassroots work — would allow the researcher to access reliable, contextually grounded data quickly, rather than starting from scratch. This positions the collaboration to move from research directly into a testable, locally validated model.

name: The Municipality of Mbombela
title: Greenfield Housing and Infrastructure Master Plan for Mbombela
summary: In the Municipality of Mbombela, a severe housing backlog forces thousands into informal settlements, while the legal requirement to equip land with basic utilities consumes roughly 60% of the municipal budget, stalling housing delivery. To solve this financial and spatial bottleneck, this project proposes a localized master plan and flexible zoning framework for greenfield land—which offers a significantly more cost-effective canvas to develop from scratch while delivering greater long-term spatial benefits to local households. By utilizing compact, mixed-use zoning on greenfield sites, the design seamlessly integrates residential units with commercial hubs, schools, healthcare, and public transit, shortening utility networks to drastically lower upfront municipal infrastructure costs. Furthermore, the plan establishes a Public-Private Partnership framework that pairs fast-tracked municipal land release and policy certainty with private sector capital, design innovation, and construction expertise. Ultimately, this initiative yields a financially sustainable urban model that accelerates formal housing delivery, slashes resident commuting costs, and attracts private investment to Mbombela.
keywords: Greenfield Land Development, Urban Master Planning, Inclusive Flexible Zoning
rationale: An ETH researcher would be vital for this project because their expertise in complex spatial-economic systems and infrastructure cost optimization can provide the rigorous empirical modeling standard planning lacks. While typical operational approaches deliver immediate designs, an ETH researcher brings specialized skills in spatial data analysis, land-use optimization, and fiscal impact modeling to test and identify optimal density thresholds for minimizing utility network costs. Rigorous scientific research can reveal long-term financial trade-offs that standard operations might miss, ensuring that our proposed flexible zoning and Public-Private Partnership frameworks can be scientifically validated, financially resilient, and scalable.
role: As local project leads, our value lies in bridging scientific innovation with ground-level execution. We offer direct access to Mbombela’s municipal networks, spatial datasets, key public-private stakeholders, and dedicated staff time to facilitate field activities and ground research models in real-world policy, regulatory, and community realities. Meanwhile, our ideal ETH researcher brings specialized expertise in sustainable urban spatial economics, quantitative urban modeling, and infrastructure cost-efficiency evaluation. They will lead technical simulations to stress-test our proposed compact zoning and utility network configurations against diverse urban growth scenarios. With ETH’s analytical rigor and our local data access and institutional reach, we believe this collaboration can transform spatial research into a scalable, financially sustainable framework for greenfield housing delivery.

name: Local South
title: From Surplus to System Change: Scaling Circular Food Innovation
summary:
Cape Town face the challenge of large volumes of edible food and nutritious by-products going to landfill, while many residents experience food insecurity and poor nutrition. Our 50% Surplus concept explores how ingredients that are normally discarded or overlooked can be transformed into nutritious, desirable and affordable foods.
We seek an ETH partner to help develop this into an urban research project that investigates how circular food innovation can strengthen Cape Town’s food system, support new local value chains, and connect producers, researchers, businesses, communities and government. The project would combine practical experimentation with selected surplus streams, consumer and community testing, and research into the institutional, market and policy conditions needed for uptake.
Success would mean viable products and pathways to market, stronger collaboration across the urban food system, and a replicable model showing how cities can turn underused food resources into nutrition, economic opportunity and wider urban resilience.
keywords: circular economy, energy, food loss & waste
rationale: We have begun testing how underused food streams can be turned into viable products, but lack the research capacity to understand how these innovations interact with the wider urban food system. An ETH researcher would help us move beyond individual product experimentation to analyse flows, actors, incentives and barriers across Cape Town’s food system, and rigorously assess where circular food innovation could have the greatest impact. We are particularly interested in expertise in urban food systems, circular economy, systems analysis and evaluation, helping us generate evidence that can inform both practical implementation and pathways for replication in other cities.
role: Local South would bring the 50% Surplus concept, existing product experimentation, local food-system knowledge and the relationships needed to test ideas in practice. We can provide access to food producers and surplus streams, community and market-testing sites, and networks across local government, academia, civil society and the food sector. We would lead local coordination, stakeholder engagement, practical experimentation and the translation of research findings into implementable actions. We would ideally work with a researcher bringing expertise in urban food systems, circular economy and systems research, complemented by methods such as material-flow analysis, stakeholder and value-chain mapping, and evaluation of social, economic and environmental outcomes. Together, the collaboration would combine rigorous research with real-world experimentation, generating evidence that is both academically robust and directly useful to Cape Town and potentially other Global South cities.

name: Kyiv Regional Development Agency
title: Scalable decision-support model for prioritising municipal energy investments in war-affected regions: the Kyiv Region pilot
summary: Municipalities in the Kyiv Region — including Bucha, Borodianka and Makariv — hold dozens of urgent energy investment needs (solar for hospitals and water utilities, cogeneration, deep renovation), but lack a systematic way to decide which projects to prepare first under conditions of blackouts, damaged infrastructure, limited budgets and security risk. Decisions today are made ad hoc, and donors receive fragmented, non-comparable proposals. The project will co-develop with an ETH Domain group a decision-support model that scores and sequences municipal energy investments by resilience impact, energy savings, feasibility and community vulnerability, and test it on our real portfolio of 20+ projects across 69 municipalities. Success means: a validated, transferable model adopted by the regional agency and integrated into the Kyiv Regional Development Strategy 2028–2034; at least 10 municipalities using it; and a replication guide for other Ukrainian regions. RDAKR provides data, municipal access and institutional uptake.
keywords: municipal energy investment, decision-support model, energy resilience, war-affected communities, regional governance
rationale: Our gap is methodological, we know our projects, but we have no validated way to weigh resilience, energy, cost and vulnerability criteria against each other under uncertainty — existing municipal energy planning tools assume stable grids and predictable budgets, which wartime Ukraine does not have. A consultant would rank our current list; a researcher can build a transferable model, test its assumptions on real data, quantify trade-offs and make it defensible to donors and financiers. We need expertise in energy systems modelling, multi-criteria decision analysis and resilience assessment, applied in a systematic, peer-reviewable way.
role: Ideal researcher: an ETH Domain group in energy systems, urban infrastructure resilience or decision science, with experience in multi-criteria assessment, scenario modelling and applied work with local governments.  What RDAKR offers: a real, documented portfolio of 20+ municipal energy investment projects with technical and cost data, including objects with completed feasibility studies; SECAP data for 10 municipalities; direct, standing access to all 69 municipalities of the region through our engagement platform and to regional decision-makers (the Agency is founded by the Kyiv Oblast Council and Administration); field sites in war-affected communities (Bucha, Borodianka) for validation; a project coordinator (Head of International Projects) and a community engagement officer as staff time; institutional uptake — integration of the model into the Kyiv Regional Development Strategy 2028–2034 and into our regional Project Development Unit for sustainable-energy investments; and dissemination to the network of Ukrainian regional development agencies.

name: MindGuard AG
title: Verified Resilience: A Digital Platform for Ukraine's Recovery
summary: MindGuard is a free mobile stress-resilience platform open to all Ukrainians, including Defenders and civilians affected by the war. It's structured around three pillars: Body, Mind, and Soul. Users complete verified physical activities, including exercises done with a buddy and in-person meetups, gamified habit-building challenges, and Soul practices like breathing exercises and art therapy, all reinforcing social bonding and reducing isolation. Completed actions earn coin rewards. In the free version, coins unlock in-app features; for B2B partners, employers finance an extended coin layer that gives their employees monetary rewards on top, turning resilience support into an employee benefit. This project would research how to design and evidence this employer-financed model so it scales sustainably, and measure its impact on users' resilience and reintegration into daily life and work.
keywords: stress resilience, social reintegration, employer-financed wellbeing, verified physical activity, Ukraine recovery
rationale: MindGuard has engagement and coin-reward data, but no rigorous evidence of its actual physiological or behavioural impact. We lack the internal expertise to design a valid study measuring outcomes like cortisol levels, sleep quality, and resilience over time, or to isolate the platform's effect from other factors in someone's life. An ETH-domain researcher would bring study design, biostatistics, and outcome-measurement expertise our team doesn't have, turning anecdotal engagement data into credible evidence we can use to convince employers and funders the model genuinely works.
role: MindGuard offers a live deployment already active across Ukraine, a real field site rather than a simulated one. We can provide platform data on user engagement, activity completion, and behavioural patterns to ground the research empirically. We also bring a growing network of Ukrainian employer partners who could serve as delivery channels and potential recruitment sites for a study. On the ground, our Ukraine-based team can handle logistics, translation, and coordination between Defenders, civilians, employers, and the research process, and commit staff time to support data collection and implementation of whatever protocol the researcher designs. What we're looking for in return is subject-matter expertise in resilience and behavioural outcome measurement, along with study design and evaluation methods we don't currently have in-house.

name: Think Playgrounds Social Enterprise (TPG)
title: Piloting Urban Biodiversity Enrichment through Nature-based Solutions for Policy Advocacy in Hanoi
summary:
Hanoi faces severe urban heat islands and climate impacts, yet Nature-based Solutions (NbS) and urban biodiversity are missing from spatial planning policies, which still favor grey infrastructure. 
Our objective is to pilot a "biodiversity enrichment" model in an existing urban park to establish a baseline and test NbS interventions for policy advocacy.
Our proposed approach: Co-designing an experimental enrichment plot with local authorities and the community, with ecological surveys and socio-behavioral assessments of community space usage. We will conduct participatory workshops to source, propagate, and nurse native plants locally, with citizen science and sensors to monitor microclimate, flora, and fauna changes.
Success will be defined by a visually compelling, scientifically backed pilot model, an active community co-management mechanism, a simple monitoring protocol, a comprehensive final report (documenting implementation, evaluation, and recommendations), and a policy brief demonstrating the feasibility of urban biodiversity.
keywords: Urban Biodiversity; Nature-based Solutions; Citizen Science; Policy Advocacy; Environmental Monitoring.
rationale: While TPG excels in community engagement and on-the-ground implementation, we lack the scientific rigor required to measure complex ecological indicators. An ETH Domain researcher is crucial to establish robust pre-intervention baselines, deploy reliable environmental monitoring, and validate citizen-generated data. We need their academic expertise to translate raw field data into compelling, evidence-based policy briefs that can convince local authorities to formally integrate NbS into urban planning frameworks.
role: Expertise needed: An ETH Domain researcher specializing in Urban Ecology, Nature-based Solutions, or Environmental Policy. What TPG offers: TPG brings over 10 years of experience upgrading 200+ public spaces across Vietnam, including 4+ years transforming a polluted riverfront into a biodiversity conservation and nature-education area. We have established 3 urban forest parks (Hanoi & Hoi An) and published key resources on inclusive design and community-based management. For this project, we offer an existing urban park as the experimental site. Leveraging our robust community mobilization capacity, we will lead local coordination, execute physical NbS interventions, and facilitate citizen science training. Partnering with HealthBridge Vietnam and the Hanoi Association of Architects, we ensure our practical implementations directly influence municipal urban governance and policy advocacy.

name: Institut Teknologi Bandung
title: The role of digital technology in shaping aspirations for spatial planning at the rural-urban interface
summary: Urban-rural transformation has reshaped rural areas as well as rural livelihoods. However, the voice of rural communities often remains marginal; they have limited opportunities to articulate their aspirations. Moreover, policies related to urban-rural transformation are frequently formulated through an urban-oriented perspective. This creates potential spatial inequalities and produces transformation that does not reflect local needs. What is at stake is not only whether rural communities benefit from the transformation but also whether they have the capacity to influence the decision-making process of the transformation policies. Digital technologies offer an opportunity to bridge the gap by connecting rural communities to the decision-making process across geographical and institutional boundaries. This project aims to explore how digital technology can mediate rural community participation in urban-rural transformation policy, co-design new forms of collaboration between stakeholders, and pilot applied research on how digital technology can bridge rural communities and the decision-making process in spatial planning at the rural-urban interface.
keywords: Urban-rural transformation, digital technology, participatory planning, e-governance
rationale: A researcher from the ETH domain is important for the project to evaluate digital participation and e-government approaches that enable meaningful public participation in the decision-making process. This project needs research expertise to understand digital platforms for an effective participatory process connecting rural communities and the decision-making process in urban-rural transformation. This goes beyond the technical development; it requires not only rigorous research but also testing and evaluating how the platform can create meaningful and inclusive participation of rural communities to influence urban-rural transformation.
role: The ideal researcher from the ETH domain would contribute expertise in digital participation and e-government, the design and evaluation of digital participation hat enable rural communities to engage in meaningful participation. It would complement my research background in rural digitalization, urban-rural transformation, as well as my understanding of Indonesia’s urban and rural contexts. I can contribute by accessing the field site and communities, collecting data, building networks with relevant local stakeholders, and providing time for fieldwork, community engagement, and pilot implementation. These complementary capacities will enable this project to co-design and test a context-specific approach in which digital technology can bridge rural communities’ aspiration with urban-rural transformation decision-making process.

name: Public Union "Taste Route of Prykarpattia"
title: The "Dykorosy" (Wild Harvest)
summary:
Problem: 56% of Ivano-Frankivsk region’s population lives in rural areas, with 30% located in mountain settlements lacking job opportunities. The war has exacerbated economic vulnerability: 18% of women have no personal income, and 43% face severe income drops. At stake is family resilience and the economic survival of mountain communities.

Goal: Empower women economically across 240 mountain settlements while fostering sustainable regional development.

Approach: Establishing a Women’s Agricultural Extension Center that integrates female leadership, mentoring, and practical training in sustainable harvesting, processing, and commercialization of wild plants and herbs, leveraging the region's 46% forest coverage.

Key to Success: Transforming traditional foraging into viable micro-enterprises through knowledge transfer, cooperation, and market access. This drives self-employment, strengthens social cohesion, and unlocks the untapped economic potential of the Carpathian region.
keywords: Rural development, wild produce, women's leadership, agricultural extension, economic resilience.
