rationale: Local operations can manage harvesting, but we lack rigorous scientific data on sustainable yield limits, active compound stability, and ecological impact under changing climate conditions. A consultant offers quick fixes; an ETH domain researcher brings standardized biochemical analysis, ecological modeling, and sustainable processing frameworks.  We specifically require expertise in natural product chemistry and sustainable resource management to quantify chemical profiles of wild plants, establish safe harvesting thresholds, and validate processing protocols. This scientific rigor bridges the gap between traditional foraging and high-value, market-compliant products, ensuring long-term ecological sustainability and economic viability for mountain communities.
role: What we offer:Field sites & primary data: Direct access to 240 mountain communities, forest gathering zones, and rural women's networks.  Operational capacity: Dedicated staff time, local infrastructure and organizing power.  In-kind support: Facilitation of sample collection, stakeholder mobilization, and hosting field visits.  What our ideal researcher brings:Subject matter expertise: Specialized knowledge in natural product chemistry, plant biochemistry, and sustainable agro-ecology.Methodologies: Standardized lab testing, chemical profiling of wild superfoods, and environmental yield modeling.Together, we translate high-level ETH research into practical, sustainable micro-enterprises, ensuring that scientific insights directly drive economic empowerment and resource conservation in the Carpathians.

name: U-Nation
title: URBAN INNOVATION INTEGRATION ACCELERATOR FOR UKRAINE. From Global Technologies to Scalable Urban Solutions
summary:
Ukrainian cities face severe infrastructure damage and energy instability; however, rebuilding individual facilities without systemic integration risks locking municipalities into fragmented and costly systems. Although international and Ukrainian companies offer promising technologies, a persistent gap remains between the availability of technologies and a city's capacity to integrate, finance, and scale them.

This project aims to bridge this integration gap by creating a science-based mechanism and the Urban Innovation Integration Readiness Index (UIIRI) to accelerate sustainable urban recovery.

Our approach combines a research accelerator (selecting 24–30 technologies), cross-system testing within U-Nation’s Smart City Living Lab, and the co-creation of Urban Integration Roadmaps with Urban Bureau in partner municipalities.

Success means a validated UIIRI assessment tool, 8–12 evaluated deep-integration case studies, applied municipal roadmaps, and a Replication Toolkit to ensure broader and scalable technology deployment across Ukraine.
keywords: Urban Innovation Integration, UIIRI Readiness Index, Smart City Living Lab, Sustainable Infrastructure Reconstruction, Municipal Validation.
rationale: Traditional operational accelerators or consultants focus on commercial maturity through Technology Readiness Level metrics or rapid pilots without analyzing systemic barriers. There is a methodological gap in the scientific assessment of cross-system compatibility (energy, water, construction, digitalization). We rely on the researcher from the ETH domain network to provide scientific leadership as Principal Investigator, drive the development of a fundamentally mathematical and empirically validated UIIRI Index, establish a methodology for evaluating 11 dimensions of technology readiness, and guarantee scientific independence, algorithmic rigor, and international-level publications.
role: ETH Researcher Expertise: Academic leadership, research methodology, development and validation of the UIIRI Index, comparative analysis of data from two cohorts, and scientific reporting.  U-Nation: Accelerator operational management, international technology scouting (24–30 solutions), provision of the Smart City Living Lab research infrastructure in Western Ukraine for cross-system testing, ecosystem engagement, and coordination.  Urban Bureau: Expertise in urban planning and systemic integration, assessment of infrastructure interfaces, and support for the development of Urban Integration Roadmaps.  Municipalities: 3–5 Ukrainian cities providing the demand, context, operational insights, and validation environment.  Resources: Co-funding (CHF 150,000), expert working time, and expertise in Ukrainian legislation and infrastructure.

name: Institute of Architecture and Urban & Spatial Planning of Serbia
title: Soft planning and territorial strategy implementation in Serbia and Switzerland
summary: In line with the multilevel governance framework for developing policy instruments based on participatory practice, Serbia has introduced soft and integrated planning approach in formation of territorial strategies contributing to sustainable urban development, alongside the statutory planning system. The project addresses the transition from the participatory formation of territorial strategies to their implementation. It examines how soft planning approaches and generated knowledge, partnerships, values and project ideas, can be further integrated into local urban planning and governance. Co-development and learning from strategy implementation cases from Serbia and Switzerland gives opportunity to explore how different institutional capacities, professional competencies and planning and governance arrangements enable a vision-oriented approach, strong relationships between strategic measures and priority areas of spatial intervention, timely preparation and stakeholder involvement. The expected results are a transferable framework for moving from strategy development towards coordination, implementation, and investment, as well as strengthened capacities of practitioners to facilitate such processes.
keywords: implementation, soft planning, sustainable urban development, urban governance, territorial strategy
rationale: Switzerland local planning and governance context offers a relevant field for learning, in which informal planning practices are embedded in institutionalised planning and governance system. ETH-domain researchers are examining how informal planning emerges within strategic spatial planning processes (ETH SPUR-led Metro-ROK), or how to better integrate community needs in planning (ETH-HTW-led User-driven Design for Future Cities). Although it is assumed that differences exist between countries in terms of the rigor of legislation, capacity to accommodate soft approaches and integrate them into the planning system, as well as the notion of soft planning as temporary or permanent, such collaboration would provide an opportunity to develop transferable approaches reflecting the value system, tradition, norms and practice supporting sustainable urban development, relevant and timely for practitioners in Serbia.
role: Building on experience with participatory formation of the national Sustainable Urban Development Strategy of Serbia until 2030 (2019) and the Study on the Unique Identity of Urban Area for implementation of the Territorial Strategy for the City of Užice and surrounding municipalities (2024-25), IAUS offers practice-based expertise in soft planning, participatory planning, strategy formation and implementation, and place-based and integrated urban and territorial development. IAUS can contribute in-situ knowledge based on real-life examples, facilitation, staff, networks, relevant cases, access to stakeholders, and qualitative and quantitative data. The collaboration would explore how soft planning mobilises place-based knowledge, resources and actors; influences institutional, procedural and governance conditions; and translates participatory priorities and project ideas into implementable actions, investment projects and planning decisions.

name: IMPACT Initiatives
title: Accessibility of Basic Urban Public Services: Identifying Gaps for More Resilient Service Delivery
summary: Dnipropetrovska Oblast is the most urbanized region in Ukraine (over 80%), economically significant, serving as a major logistics hub, hosting a large population of IDPs. Ensuring equitable access to essential public services is therefore critical to urban resilience, social cohesion, and recovery. The project will assess accessibility of basic services in 3 cities through complementary lenses: spatial and social. GIS and administrative data will be used to identify gaps in access to healthcare, education, administrative, social services, utilities. Qualitative research will examine key barriers faced by different population groups in cities. Key outputs: comprehensive city accessibility profiles, actionable recommendations and a replicable methodology for other municipalities. Success will mean that participating cities integrate findings into local recovery and development plans. Knowledge transfer to and use of the results by the practice partner (Dnipro Regional State Administration) uses the methodology to scale evidence-based accessibility assessments and support improvements to regional policies.
keywords: basic services, urban resilience, accessibility, spatial analysis
rationale: We need expert support to frame a research approach to assessing basic public service accessibility in an urban context, focusing on spatial and social accessibility. We need to identify other relevant dimensions and appropriate methods, including spatial analysis and research with service users. Based on the expert’s recommendations, our team will develop survey and data-collection tools for the social accessibility component, which the expert will review. We also need the expert to help interpret findings and develop evidence-based recommendations. Key skills: mixed-methods research, accessibility analysis, urban services, spatial analysis, research design, and quantitative and qualitative data interpretation.
role: Our team combines multidisciplinary expertise in GIS, sociological research and area-based recovery planning with significant field research capacity and established relationships with local and regional authorities. These networks can facilitate case-study selection, access to relevant administrative and spatial data, engagement with service providers and residents, and participatory validation of findings. Drawing on IMPACT’s extensive applied research experience in Ukraine, RSPU staff will contribute directly to research design, data collection and GIS analysis across participating cities. Complementing the ETH researcher’s advanced expertise in urban accessibility, spatial modelling and research design, we will help ensure that the methodology is robust yet practical for Ukrainian local and regional authorities to apply and transferable to other urban contexts.

name: Technical University of Cluj-Napoca
title: Cost allocation and governance of distributed solar in a Romanian city.
summary: Romania added 360 000 rooftop solar prosumers in 6 years, over 4,000 MW. Under current settlement rules, prosumers are compensated in energy volumes and are fully shielded from the cost their unpredictable output imposes on the system. That cost does not disappear; it accumulates with the party carrying balance responsibility and is recovered through supply tariffs paid by everyone. Nobody has measured this transfer, and cities subsidizing rooftop solar are doing so blind. Working with Cluj-Napoca municipality and a company operating over 400 installations, this pilot will build a first dataset linking metered prosumer output to settlement outcomes, produce an initial estimate of the transfer, and convene local stakeholders to define what municipalities need to govern it. Success will be measured by a defensible first estimate of the transfer, an established research-practice partnership, and a problem definition agreed with local stakeholders that can anchor a subsequent full research grant.
keywords: distributed energy resources, cost allocation, prosumers
rationale: Quantifying how much of the system cost of distributed solar is shifted onto non-prosuming households requires a method that does not yet exist. Metered output must be linked to settlement outcomes under a conditional pricing regime, and the resulting transfer attributed across consumer groups, a question of causal attribution and distributional analysis rather than of data processing. The results are intended to inform municipal policy, which requires a method that is methodologically transparent and independently verifiable. We seek expertise in energy system modeling and in the distributional evaluation of energy policy.
role: We bring three assets that are difficult to assemble from outside the country. First, data: a partner company operating over 400 photovoltaic installations totaling 5–6 MW, most with bidirectional metering recorded at five-minute resolution since commissioning, representing roughly 5% of the prosumer capacity of Cluj County. Second, access: an established working relationship with the Cluj-Napoca municipality, including its energy manager, with whom we have collaborated on previous proposals, and familiarity with the Romanian regulatory framework and its published settlement data. Third, research capacity: a group at the Technical University of Cluj-Napoca working on forecasting and artificial intelligence applied to power systems, able to contribute staff time, doctoral supervision, and local fieldwork.  From the ETH partner we would value expertise in energy system modeling, in distributional and welfare analysis of energy policy, and in designing studies whose results are usable by public authorities.

name: IMPACT Initiatives
title: Asessment of the Local Capacity for Urban Recovery and Long-Term Resilience
summary:
Cities across Ukraine face diverse but interconnected challenges, from resilience to strategic and recovery planning. There is limited systematic understanding of existing capacities, specific knowledge and skills gaps, and which capacities should be developed within municipalities or complemented by other actors. This research will address this gap by assessing capacities (including skills/competencies) in 5–9 cities in Dnipro region.
Key outputs: Local Recovery & Resilience Capacity Framework, city-level capacity profiles, recommendations for targeted training/capacity-building programmes that could potentially be supported by the state, donors and development partners.
Success will mean that participating cities integrate the findings into programmes aimed at strengthening the capacity and competencies of local actors, and that the practice partner (Dnipro Regional State Administration) uses the methodology to scale up programmes for strengthening the capacity and competencies of communities in region in accordance with the official state Index of Capacity and Digital Transformation of Communities.
keywords: Local recovery, capacities, skills, urban governance, digitalization
rationale: An ETH-domain researcher is crucial to rigorously assess and compare urban governance capacities, skills and institutional conditions across cities. Their expertise would help ensure comparability across cases and distinguish structural factors from context-specific challenges. This is essential to move beyond case diagnosis toward evidence-based findings that can inform scalable capacity-building programmes. The researcher would strengthen the Local Recovery & Resilience Capacity Framework and connect local evidence with broader research and international practice on urban resilience and recovery.
role: IMPACT brings detailed knowledge of the challenges and bottlenecks undermining effective urban recovery in Ukraine, supported by an extensive track record of engagement with local authorities, applied research, and capacity building initiatives. We will provide field capacity, stakeholder networks and staff capacity for research design, institutional mapping, mixed methods data collection and participatory validation processes. The ETH researcher would contribute expertise in urban governance, institutional capacity assessments, and advanced research methods, enabling the project to understand how individual skills, organisational structures, information management practices, and institutional relationships shape municipal urban recovery capacity. Together with Dnipro Regional State Administration, we will translate this evidence into a framework for prioritising capacity development that can support regional programming.

name: KreativaLab
title: Library Incubators: Aligned Public-Private Governance for Affordable Urban Co-Working in Serbia
summary: Skyrocketing real estate costs in Belgrade and Novi Sad price out early-stage entrepreneurs, stifling local urban innovation. This pilot project explores transforming underutilized public libraries in Serbia into affordable co-working spaces and innovation hubs. Serbia has over 600 public libraries with branches, as by law each municipality must have a library. This resource remains poorly used in the times of innovations-driven economies, which this pilot tackles. Operating under the Finance & Urban Governance domain, we aim to research and design a sustainable public-private financing framework that aligns municipal infrastructure with private tech sponsorships. In collaboration with local Serbian municipal partners, we will conduct spatial feasibility assessments, demand-driven stakeholder workshops, and comparative analyses utilizing Swiss models like Zurich's PBZ network or Universität Zürich LiRI infrastructure. Success means delivering an actionable blueprint for a self-sustaining library incubator model and cementing a robust research consortium prepared for a full-scale Urban Research Grant application.
keywords: Public-Private Partnerships (PPP), Urban Development, Affordable Co-working, Library Transformation, Municipal Asset Optimization
rationale: An ETH domain researcher is crucial to bridge the knowledge gap between Swiss public value management and Serbia’s transitional municipal framework. While consultants offer generic templates, rigorous academic research reveals how to structurally align public-private incentives without eroding civic trust. We require an ETH researcher’s specific expertise in urban financial modeling, institutional policy design, and socio-spatial analysis. Their objective methodology will uncover systemic funding risks and space-utilization behavioral patterns. This high-level academic rigor is vital to co-develop a scalable, self-sustaining library incubator model that day-to-day municipal operations simply cannot formulate.
role: As the local practice partner based in culture and creative industries domain, KreativaLab provides the essential on-the-ground execution, institutional networks, and local context required to make this research viable. We offer direct access to public library field sites in Belgrade and Novi Sad and existing data on regional library infrastructure and spatial limitations. Additionally, we will dedicate staff time to facilitate community stakeholder focus groups and manage local project logistics. While we anchor the project locally, our ideal ETH researcher brings advanced subject matter expertise in urban real estate economics, spatial modeling, and public-private finance governance. They will provide the rigorous, objective methodology, such as financial feasibility modeling and comparative policy evaluation, needed to translate raw local data into a scalable framework. Together, our collaboration blends top-tier academic theory with local operational realities to create a truly demand-oriented, sustainable urban solution.

name: City of Cape Town
title: Climate risk, insurance impacts and infrastructure resilience
summary:
Climate change is expected to reshape infrastructure costs, risk exposure, and insurance markets. Research would assess how climate hazards affect municipal assets, households, public liability and insurability (for the municipality and residents), informing adaptation investments and resilience planning across the city.

Given increasing disaster / climate change impact – what is the current 1) cost of inaction, 2) cost of action (specifically adaptation), 3) funding mechanisms to fund risk mitigation investment (i.e. the resilience funding gap).
keywords: Climate Insurance Climate resilient planning Climate funding
rationale: Cape Town faces growing exposure to floods, fire, drought and coastal erosion, yet we cannot quantify what this costs the City and its residents, or what adaptation interventions would save (i.e. avoided costs). Our data on assets, insurance claims, public liability and service disruptions sits in separate systems and is rarely linked to hazard models. Consultants deliver one-off studies; we need a rigorous, transferable method that integrates probabilistic hazard modelling, asset vulnerability, insurance and liability economics, and fiscal analysis. An ETH researcher brings the modelling depth, independence and scientific credibility to estimate the costs of inaction and action, and to size the resilience funding gap.
role: Our ideal researcher would bring expertise in climate and natural hazard risk modelling, infrastructure vulnerability assessment and risk financing or insurance economics, including catastrophe modelling and cost-benefit analysis of adaptation. Experience in Global South cities and co-produced research would be valuable.  The City of Cape Town's Research and Resilience Branches (in the Future Planning and Resilience Directorate) would anchor the partnership and coordinate across line departments, including Disaster Risk Management, Finance (Risk and Insurance), Water and Sanitation and Climate Change. We can offer: - Data: municipal asset registers, insurance and claims records, disaster incident data, capital budget information, climate change risk modelling and spatial/GIS layers. - Staff time: our in-house researchers and departmental specialists. - Field sites and networks: hazard-exposed areas, including informal settlements, plus links to national government, insurers and city networks.  Findings could inform capital prioritisation, climate adaptation planning and the City's resilience financing framework and approach.

name: Daba.Cities
title: Dar.AI Compact City Pilot: Validating AI-Assisted Parcel-Level Planning for Urban Densification in Casablanca
summary: Casablanca continues to expand while many serviced inner-city parcels remain underused. Planning rules are dispersed across zoning documents and interpreted manually, making it difficult to compare development capacity consistently or identify where infill can absorb growth. Daba.Cities proposes a 12-month Urban Pilot Project to co-develop and validate a research-grade decision-support method that converts zoning rules into parcel-level buildable-capacity scenarios. Building on digitized zoning data for nine Moroccan cities and an existing Python engine, the pilot will test 30–50 parcels across contrasting Casablanca urban fabrics, compare automated outputs with expert interpretation, and assess usefulness for densification, housing-capacity and land-use-efficiency decisions. Success will be a validated benchmark dataset, documented error/accuracy profile, stakeholder-tested prototype, methodological paper/brief, and a clear research plan for scaling to a larger Urban Research Grant and additional Moroccan cities.
keywords: Spatial planning; urban densification; digital planning; artificial intelligence; compact city development
rationale: Prof. Adrienne Grêt-Regamey’s PLUS group is particularly relevant because it develops digitally supported, participatory urban-planning methods, land-use decision models and decision-support platforms. Daba.Cities already has an operational regulatory engine and Moroccan zoning dataset; the research gap is rigorous validation, uncertainty/error characterization, and translation into a scientifically defensible planning method. PLUS can strengthen research design, spatial modelling and stakeholder validation, while a policy-oriented collaborator such as SPUR could complement the work on densification and planning instruments. ETH involvement would turn a promising operational tool into a tested applied-research prototype with relevance beyond individual property feasibility.
role: Daba.Cities, a Moroccan-registered environmental and social enterprise, will serve as the local practice partner and direct user of the research outputs. We will contribute digitized zoning data for nine Moroccan cities, our existing Python development engine for computing buildable envelopes, and access to surveyed underutilized city-centre properties that can serve as real pilot cases. We will provide regulatory interpretation, parcel-level data, local data collection, staff time, prototype testing and in-kind technical support. We will also facilitate access to architects, planners, property owners and urban-development stakeholders, and support validation workshops with relevant Moroccan institutions and practitioners. Our role will be to ensure that the research remains grounded in real planning and redevelopment decisions and that the resulting methodology can be integrated into Daba.Cities’ operational workflow for compact, climate-resilient city-centre regeneration.

name: Institute of Renewable Energy of the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine
title: Geothermal Framework for Resilient Urban Heating in Ukraine
summary:
Problem
Attacks on surface energy networks cause severe winter heating shortages in Ukrainian cities. There is an urgent need for secure, decentralized heating alternatives to keep basic urban services running.

Objective
To establish a validated foundation for secure, decentralized urban energy management, we propose a portfolio of geothermal solutions, including Underground Thermal Energy Storage (UTES), retrofitting depleted wells, and modernizing substations. The exact combination will be tailored to the local community's needs and the ETH researcher's expertise.

Approach
Since the grant does not fund physical construction, we will co-develop a digital twin prototype. By combining our geological data with ETH’s simulations, we will model how these geothermal methods can operate safely.

Achievement
A digital tool that helps our local non-academic practice partners modernize district heating and transition to secure, renewable geothermal energy.
keywords: geothermal energy, underground thermal storage, well retrofitting, district heating, digital twin
rationale: While we possess local geological data and community connections, we lack the advanced computational modeling required to test and validate outcomes for resilient heating solutions. Because establishing a framework for Underground Thermal Energy Storage (UTES) and retrofitting depleted wells involves highly unique variables, a conventional consultancy assignment is insufficient. We specifically require an ETH Domain researcher’s scientific rigor to co-develop a validated methodology, rather than merely specifying designs for a single site. This research will empower our local practice partners to successfully deliver and roll out these vital public services at scale.
role: Working alongside our local non-academic practice partners (such as city councils, territorial communities, and utility companies), our institute will make sure the ETH's solutions are properly adapted to Ukrainian realities. We will provide existing geological data, help gather new field data, and manage on-site coordination to the extent possible for a research organization. Crucially, our team will process this data to adapt ETH's standard economic and operational models so they actually work in practice for Ukraine's specific needs.

name: "Bila Tserkva Centre for Comprehensive Rehabilitation of Persons with Disabilities SHANS"
title: Barrier-Free Recovery: Inclusive Public Services and Spaces for Veterans, People with Disabilities and Their Caregivers in Bila Tserkva
summary:
Bila Tserkva is home to an estimated 20,000–25,000 veterans, and 53% of residents find the city inconvenient for people with limited mobility. Recovery efforts address only physical access; psychological barriers – trauma triggers, anxiety in crowded spaces, stigma, complex bureaucracy – are ignored, so services rebuilt for veterans often remain unused. Women caring for veterans at home carry the daily burden, yet are absent from planning.
Objective: make public services and spaces usable for veterans, people with disabilities and their caregivers. Approach: together with the municipal rehabilitation centre SHANS, combine clinical psychology and urban design to map barriers with users, co-design a barrier-free audit tool integrating physical and psychological criteria, and pilot low-cost interventions at SHANS and one other municipal service site.
Success: the tool is applied to at least five sites, SHANS staff are trained, users report easier access, and the city integrates the criteria into its Barrier-Free Programme.
keywords: barrier-free public services, veterans' reintegration, trauma-informed urban design, accessibility, caregivers
rationale: Together with SHANS we have direct access to veterans, people with disabilities and caregivers, local trust and clinical psychology expertise. What holds us back is the missing link between psychology and urban design: we can see that people avoid services, but cannot systematically measure how the built environment and service design cause this, or prove which changes work. A consultant could audit ramps; rigorous research can turn psychological barriers into validated design criteria and evaluate interventions. We need an ETH researcher skilled in urban design or spatial planning, participatory co-design, spatial analysis and evaluation methods.
role: Together with SHANS we have direct access to veterans, people with disabilities and caregivers, local trust and clinical psychology expertise. What holds us back is the missing link between psychology and urban design: we can see that people avoid services, but cannot systematically measure how the built environment and service design cause this, or prove which changes work. A consultant could audit ramps; rigorous research can turn psychological barriers into validated design criteria and evaluate interventions. We need an ETH researcher skilled in urban design or spatial planning, participatory co-design, spatial analysis and evaluation methods.

name: Municipal Institution of Bila Tserkva City Council "Territorial Centre for Social Services named after Peter Novotny"
title: Age-Friendly Recovery: Safe Routes, Accessible Shelters and Meeting Places for Older People in Bila Tserkva
summary:
Older people are the least visible victims of the war: they account for half of civilian deaths in Ukraine, a third lack safe shelter, and 44% of those over 70 live alone. In Bila Tserkva, 53% of residents find the city inconvenient for people with limited mobility. Missing benches and lighting, stairs to shelters, blackouts and digital-only services keep older people at home, increasing loneliness and anxiety.
Objective: make one micro-district safer and easier to use for older people. Approach: together with the Territorial Centre for Social Services, audit everyday routes and shelters with older people, measure loneliness and perceived safety, co-design improvements and pilot a "route of rest", one accessible shelter and a meeting place that also works during blackouts.
Success: one route and shelter improved, weekly use of the meeting place, reduced loneliness among participants, and the city adopting an age-friendly checklist.
keywords: age-friendly city, older people, walkability, accessible shelters, loneliness
rationale: The Territorial Centre knows older people's needs and reaches those living alone through home care, and we bring clinical psychology expertise. What we lack is the link to urban design and mobility research: we cannot measure systematically how routes, shelters and public spaces keep older people at home, or prove which changes work. A consultant could list missing benches; rigorous research can link environmental barriers to loneliness and mobility and evaluate interventions. We need an ETH researcher skilled in walkability and mobility analysis, spatial cognition or urban design, participatory methods and evaluation.
role: Ideal researcher: expertise in walkability and mobility of older people, spatial cognition or urban design; methods for route and accessibility audits, spatial analysis, participatory design and before–after evaluation. We offer: direct access to older people through the Territorial Centre's day services and home care, including those who live alone and rarely go out; social workers' time for recruitment, home visits and co-design workshops; premises for the meeting place and workshops; service data on clients' needs (anonymised); links to the city's Department of Social Protection and the Barrier-Free Programme, which can fund physical improvements. Our academic partner, Prof. [removed] [removed] (MAUP), contributes clinical psychology expertise, validated instruments for loneliness and anxiety, fieldwork coordination, an ethics and safeguarding protocol, and nine years of professional experience in Bila Tserkva. After the pilot we will continue the meeting place and apply the checklist in other districts.

name: Keberlanjutan utama Foundation
title: Bandung Urban Transformation: Integrating Digital Innovation and Stakeholder Engagement for Sustainable Governance
summary:
A project that aims to develop various strategies to encourage sustainable solutions to resolve various environmental problems in urban Bandung. 

These problems include water scarcity due to alternative land use that causes river and canal normalization, 

Unmanaged waste management results in water pollution, and no monitoring system or regulation on quality and spatial planning.

To implement this project, a digital transformation strategy is developed that begins with 

Establishing monitoring systems, including baseline studies and digital mapping; 
Developing monitoring systems; conducting pilot interventions; and, 

Finally, evaluating sustainability.

This project can involve various levels of participants, including governments, private institutions, and communities, and is expected to produce a sustainable environmental monitoring system.
keywords: digital mapping, monitoring systems, Conducting pilot interventions, evaluation, sustainability
rationale: The involvement of a researcher from the ETH domain is essential due to experts’ vast experience and competencies in digital transformation, sustainability, and international relations.   In this way, it is possible to secure the highest standards in research and development of the project, as well as benefit from the global knowledge and contacts of ETH experts.   This collaboration will ensure the scientific accuracy and innovation of the solution, as well as its sustainability and viability in terms of international standards.   By combining the site-specific insights and vision of a local researcher with the global perspective of an ETH expert, the project will address the most crucial environmental and urban development concerns of Bandung.
role: As part of the collaboration, our role will be to provide extensive local networks, field sites in Bandung, and staff time dedicated to the community and environmental monitoring.  As such, we would be able to provide in-kind support for the project, including providing baseline data, stakeholders’ contacts, and some expertise about the realities of the urban sustainability landscape.  Ideally, the ETH representative would have an expert-level understanding of digital transformation, environmental modelling, and evaluation areas to apply the scientific research aspects to the project’s practical needs.   With such a specialist on board, the collaboration would address the critical points of water scarcity, waste management, and river normalization to create cutting-edge solutions that would combine the digital and community aspects, follow global standards and be relevant to the local environment.

name: SEILER & SEILER
title: A Data-Driven Tool for Testing Urban Development Scenarios
summary:
Cities and planning teams need a clear way to see how much floor area could be created in planned areas and what are the consequences for infrastructure and finances. Today, these estimates are often made in spreadsheets, using different definitions and assumptions.

This project will develop and test a tool that brings together land parcel and cluster maps, zoning rules, and development scenarios in the face wartime uncertainty. Users will be able to change key settings — such as planning area boundaries or floor-area ratios — and see how these changes affect the possible floor area in each parcel or cluster. The results will support discussions across departements and negotiations with landowners. Crucially, the tool will also be usable for projecting the required investments for public infrastructure and services against the anticipated development fees, thereby ensuring that growth plans are infrastructurally viable and and foster spatial justice by aligning private developer contributions with the equitable distribution of public resources.
keywords: Urban planning, Land-use scenarios, Geospatial data, Automated Floor-area modelling
rationale: The project will combine practical experience from urban planning projects with the latest research insights from an ETH-domain researcher in urban planning and/or geospatial analysis.
role: We can contribute practical experience in urban planning and GIS development, along with a clear understanding of the decisions the tool needs to support and the challenges faced by departments and landowners. We can provide a pilot area and explain the applicable zoning rules. Together, we can translate research findings into a tool and approach that fit real planning processes and support informed discussions about development, infrastructure investment and the fair distribution of public resources.

name: Initiatives for Civic Integrations – ICI Gostivar
title: Improving drinking water quality monitoring and public trust in Gostivar
summary:
The July 2026 drinking water crisis affected Gostivar, a city of approximately 33,000 residents. Tap water was banned for drinking, and around 4,000 residents reportedly sought medical care for gastrointestinal symptoms. Households had to obtain alternative water supplies, creating additional costs and difficulties, particularly for older people, people with disabilities and low-income families. Some residents continue to avoid tap water and lack clear information about its safety.

At stake are public health, equitable access to safe water and trust in public services.

We seek an ETH Domain researcher with expertise in drinking water microbiology and monitoring to design risk-based sampling, interpret laboratory results and help evaluate public communication. Together, we aim to develop and test a scientifically grounded monitoring-and-communication approach that supports risk identification, helps residents make informed decisions and provides recommendations for institutional improvements.
keywords: Drinking water quality; water quality monitoring; risk communication; public trust; urban water governance
rationale: ICI brings fieldwork and community engagement experience but needs scientific expertise in risk-based sampling, indicator selection and microbiological interpretation. An ETH Domain researcher will co-develop the methodology, guide implementation and ensure data quality. Beyond routine compliance testing or a consultancy assessment, the pilot will systematically evaluate which measurements reveal relevant risks and which communication formats improve residents’ understanding and informed trust. We require expertise in drinking water microbiology, pathogen risk assessment and monitoring design, complemented by risk communication research. This collaboration will generate reliable evidence and a tested approach for ICI’s civic monitoring work.
role: ICI will contribute local knowledge of Gostivar, community networks and experience in field research on rivers and water resources in the Polog region. We will coordinate local activities, engage residents, support sampling under agreed protocols, and organise consultations and dissemination. Staff time, logistics and costs will be defined in the joint budget. Access to utility data and sampling points will be discussed with relevant institutions.  The researcher will bring expertise in drinking water microbiology and risk assessment. Together, we will select sampling points and indicators, establish quality assurance protocols and train the local team. The researcher will lead data analysis, interpret findings and evaluate how public information influences residents’ understanding and trust.  ICI will apply the tested approach in its environmental monitoring and public information work, while jointly developing recommendations for relevant institutions.

name: Institute for Retraining and Advanced Training of Personnel in the Field of Transport under the Ministry of Transport of the Republic of Uzbekistan
title: Strengthening Transport Workforce Skills for Safer and More Inclusive Urban Mobility
summary: Urban transport in Uzbekistan's fast-growing cities depends on the people who run it: drivers, dispatchers, metro and rail staff, and vehicle diagnostics technicians. Yet retraining programmes are rarely based on evidence of what passengers experience, where safety and service problems occur, or which skills are missing. Women, older people and people with disabilities are often most affected. This pilot will test a diagnostic approach in one city, combining passenger surveys, review of service and incident records, and a skills assessment of transport personnel. Together with ETH Domain researchers, the Institute for Retraining and Advanced Training of Personnel in the Field of Transport, under the Ministry of Transport, will turn the findings into updated retraining courses, including distance-learning modules. Success means a validated method, a clear skills-gap analysis, updated training content, and a concept for a larger multi-city Urban Research Grant
keywords: urban mobility, transport workforce skills, road safety, gender inclusion, Uzbekistan
rationale: Our Institute trains transport personnel across road, rail, metro and water transport, but lacks rigorous methods to measure how workforce skills affect service quality and safety for different passengers. Daily operations and consultants typically produce descriptive reports, not validated, comparable evidence. An ETH Domain researcher would contribute expertise in transport systems analysis, survey design, gender-sensitive data analysis, and training needs assessment. This makes our findings credible, internationally comparable, and directly usable for updating retraining programmes and preparing a larger Urban Research Grant
role: Our Institute, under the Ministry of Transport, would act as the local practice partner and the main user of the results. We offer direct access to transport personnel across road, rail, metro and water transport, who can take part in skills assessments and interviews. We can facilitate cooperation with transport operators and ministry bodies, and provide access to available service and incident records, subject to data protection rules. Our staff would contribute time for fieldwork coordination, local logistics and translation, and our training programmes and distance-learning system would be used to test and roll out updated courses. We expect the ETH Domain researcher to bring expertise in transport systems analysis, survey and evaluation methods, gender-sensitive data analysis and training needs assessment. Together we would co-design the diagnostic approach and ensure the findings lead to practical changes in national retraining programmes.

name: Researcher · EPFL
title: Scenario-based pathways for climate-resilient and low-carbon cities
summary: Rapid urban growth will profoundly reshape cities’ energy needs, climate risks and environmental conditions. This project will develop a scenario-based framework to explore alternative urban growth and decarbonization pathways and/or their implications for climate adaptation, mitigation and local energy generation (depending on local needs). Combining spatial modelling, urban climate simulations and renewable-energy assessment, we will quantify how alternative configurations of urban form, density, vegetation and transport infrastructure affect relevant indicators (e.g., heat exposure, flood risk, carbon emissions, potential for distributed solar and wind energy). The project will identify synergies and trade-offs between benefits and sectors, and evaluate alternative development scenarios with local practice partners. The resulting open and transferable decision-support tool will help cities compare pathways and identify integrated, context-specific strategies for resilient and low-carbon urban development.
keywords: Urban growth, Decarbonization, Climate Risks, Climate Adaptation, Mobility
rationale: Practice partners are essential to ensure that the project responds to real urban planning challenges and produces actionable outcomes. Municipal planning and energy or transport authorities can co-define relevant urban growth and decarbonization scenarios, provide local data and institutional knowledge, and assess the feasibility of proposed strategies. Their involvement will ensure that the modelling framework reflects actual planning constraints and decision-making processes.
role: We bring expertise in urban climate, energy, mobility and urban growth modelling, supported by state-of-the-art simulation tools. We can provide modelling capacity, spatial analysis, scenario development and interdisciplinary research expertise, as well as access to relevant datasets and computational resources.

name: Researcher · ETH Zurich
title: Planning Industrial and Logistics Development: Reconciling Economic Growth and Land-Use Efficiency
summary:
Industry and logistics areas dedicated to production, storage and distribution of goods are increasingly shaping cities and their surroundings. Worldwide, they have been the primary catalyst for land-use change over the past two decades, with demand for further development projected to rise. In both Switzerland and Vietnam, their development is highly challenging in the context of policy goals on soil protection, food security and biodiversity conservation. Yet, we currently lack knowledge on how logistics areas can be developed towards meeting economic growth goals without affecting implementation of  sustainable land use goals. 
The goal of this research is to answer the question: How can a country accommodate rapidly growing demand for industrial and logistics land while avoiding the loss and fragmentation of valuable agricultural and ecological land? Particularly relevant is an investigation of how different planning and environmental-governance systems reconcile logistics development with competing land, soil and biodiversity objectives.
Vietnam (rapid expansion of logistics and greenfield development) and Switzerland (land scarcity and increasing pressure to use land more efficiently) constitute contrasting but complementary case studies for answering this relevant question. 
In brief:
Who is affected?: Businesses and logistics operators, communities, farmers, as well as ecosystems and future generations, are affected by the growing demand for industrial and logistics land.
What's at stake? The ability to reconcile economic growth and efficient logistics with the protection of agricultural land, soils, biodiversity and ecological connectivity.
What do we hope to achieve? To generate knowledge on how planning and environmental-governance systems can guide industrial and logistics development towards more sustainable land use, drawing lessons from the contrasting cases of Vietnam and Switzerland.
keywords: economic growth, logistics and industry areas, land use efficiency goals, soil protection, biodiversity conservation
rationale: Vietnam’s Ministry of Construction provides direct expertise on how industrial and logistics development is translated into spatial planning. The Department of Planning and Architecture can contribute knowledge on planning frameworks, land-use allocation and the integration of environmental objectives into spatial planning, while the Urban Development Agency can provide practical insights and data into infrastructure development and logistics-related growth. Their involvement would ensure that research findings reflect institutional realities.  A university partner with relevant expertise in the area could greatly help implement the project.
role: Expertise needed in a practice partner: knowledge of the legal frameworks on industry and logistics development, access to relevant spatial planning documents and land use data. For this collaboration I can offer: matching funds and in-kind support, opportunity to visit study areas in Switzerland, access to all knowledge generated in the project, connection to international research networks.

name: Researcher · EPFL
countries: Indonesia; Ghana; Vietnam; Morocco; South Africa
title: Strengthening Heat Resilience in Schools and Health Facilities
summary: Extreme heat is increasingly threatening the safe and reliable operation of schools and health facilities, especially in cities where buildings and institutions may have limited capacity to cope with prolonged high temperatures. Children, patients, older people, and frontline staff are especially vulnerable, yet there exists a lack of practical ways to identify which facilities are most at risk and where adaptation efforts should be prioritized. This project is aimed to develop and test a practical framework for assessing heat vulnerability in critical public facilities and supporting locally appropriate adaptation planning. The project will work with local stakeholders to understand how heat risk is shaped by the built environment, institutional capacity, and local conditions. Success would mean enabling municipalities, and facility managers to better identify vulnerable facilities, prioritize limited resources, and take targeted actions to improve heat resilience and protect essential services.
keywords: Heat vulnerability; Urban climate adaptation; Built environment; Critical infrastructure
rationale: For this project, the practice partner is crucial because local knowledge is needed to understand how heat affects schools and health facilities, how buildings are operated, and what adaptation measures are feasible within existing institutional and resource constraints. The partner would provide access to facilities and stakeholders, contextual knowledge of urban planning and public infrastructure, and practical insight into local decision-making processes. Their involvement would ensure that the project is co-developed around real operational needs, that proposed solutions are locally appropriate, and that the resulting approach can be integrated into existing planning and adaptation processes.
role: I would bring expertise in heat vulnerability assessment, sensing, geospatial analysis, and data-driven modelling, with a particular focus on understanding how buildings and human behaviour influence exposure to extreme heat. I can contribute to the development of a scientifically robust assessment framework, indicator selection, data analysis, and evaluation of potential adaptation strategies. I would also bring experience in interdisciplinary research and in translating technical evidence into practical decision-support approaches. An ideal practice partner would complement this expertise with strong knowledge of the local urban and institutional context, access to schools and health facilities, relationships with municipalities and relevant stakeholders, and experience in implementing climate adaptation or urban resilience initiatives. Together, this would enable the project to combine scientific rigour with locally grounded, implementable solutions.

name: Researcher · ETH Zurich
title: iQ-Earth: Digitizing the urban built environment for earthquake-resilient societies
summary:
The devastating earthquakes of 2026, which claimed thousands of lives and caused major economic losses worldwide, once again exposed how vulnerable societies remain to earthquake risk—a challenge expected to intensify as urbanization accelerates and dependence on critical infrastructure grows. Yet reliably evaluating how buildings, infrastructure, and urban environments will perform before disaster strikes remains prohibitively expensive, expertise-intensive, and non-scalable.
iQ-Earth addresses this challenge through a bold vision: a future in which every asset and eventually every city has a continuously evolving digital representation capable of assessing earthquake performance in real time. Toward this vision, the project will automate earthquake-soil-structure modeling, enable scalable high-fidelity digital representation of the built environment, and demonstrate applicability to real-world cases by integrating advanced earthquake-soil-structure simulation with physics-preserving reduced-order models.
If successful, iQ-Earth will lay the foundations for asset-specific decision-making on mitigation, urban planning, preparedness, recovery, infrastructure investment, and risk transfer, ultimately creating resilient communities, reducing losses, and saving lives.
keywords: Earthquake-resilient communities; Digitalization of the built environment; High-fidelity earthquake-soil-structure simulation; Reduced-order modeling; Decision support
rationale: The project requires a practice partner responsible for disaster risk management, infrastructure management, or urban planning to ensure that the developed framework addresses real-world needs and constraints. While the central scientific challenge is to bridge fidelity and scale, transforming computationally expensive but highly accurate earthquake-soil-structure simulations into scalable representations deployable from individual assets to entire cities, successful implementation depends on access to infrastructure data and stakeholder requirements. A practice partner would co-develop relevant use cases, guide the translation of research outputs into decision-support tools, and facilitate demonstration in real urban environments, thereby maximizing impact, adoption, and societal benefit.
role: As part of this collaboration, I bring the unique expertise required to achieve the project's ambitious goals. Throughout my research, as well as through collaborations with engineering consultancies, infrastructure stakeholders, and federal agencies, I have developed expertise in the high-fidelity simulation of earthquakes, soils, structures, and their interaction, combining advanced finite-element modeling and experimental validation with high-performance computing and automated computational workflows. More recently, my research has expanded toward integrating regional seismological wave-propagation models with local high-fidelity soil-structure models, reduced-order modeling, and digital twinning through collaborations across ETH Zurich and international partners. These activities have enabled me to establish the multidisciplinary network and expertise necessary to realize iQ-Earth, uniquely positioning me to bridge high-fidelity earthquake-soil-structure simulations with scalable digital representations of the built environment. Coupled with the right practice partner, these capabilities would enable the co-development of scientifically rigorous, scalable, and practical solutions supporting decision-making before and after disaster strikes, ultimately contributing to more earthquake-resilient communities.
